fixes.answer: I strongly believe that access to decent, affordable housing is a [[fundamental human right]], not a privilege. Shelter is a basic need, and stable housing is the foundation upon which people build healthy, productive lives. When housing becomes unaffordable, it drives inequality, homelessness and [[hardship]]. So I think governments have a clear responsibility to ensure that housing is available and affordable to all, treating it as an essential rather than a mere [[commodity]].
fixes.why: 'affordable' and 'essential' are plain; marked 'fundamental human right' and 'hardship'

fixes.answer: Both have their advantages, depending on circumstances. Owning a home offers stability, security and the chance to build wealth over time, which is why many [[aspire to]] it. Renting, however, offers greater flexibility and freedom from the burdens of maintenance and large [[mortgages]], which suits those who value mobility. So there is no universal answer; it depends on one's financial situation, life stage and how much stability versus flexibility one [[prioritises]].
fixes.why: 'stability' and 'flexibility' are plain; marked 'aspire to' and 'mortgages'

fixes.answer: The high cost is driven by a fundamental imbalance between supply and demand. As people [[flock to]] cities for work, demand for housing soars, while the supply of new homes often fails to keep pace due to limited land and slow construction. Property speculation and foreign investment can also inflate prices. So it is largely a matter of high demand meeting [[constrained]] supply, made worse by [[speculation]], pushing prices beyond ordinary people's reach.

A housing shortage has [[far-reaching]] social consequences. It drives up rents and prices, forcing people to spend a huge portion of their income on housing, which deepens financial stress and inequality. It can lead to overcrowding, longer commutes, and in severe cases, homelessness. It may also prevent young people from becoming independent. So a lack of affordable housing genuinely [[undermines]] [[social mobility]] and the overall wellbeing of a community.
fixes.why: 'wellbeing' is plain; marked 'far-reaching' and the phrase 'social mobility'

fixes.answer: I anticipate several developments. To address shortages and sustainability, we may see more compact, [[high-density]] and eco-friendly housing, along with innovative solutions like modular or [[prefabricated]] homes. Smart-home technology will likely become standard. There may also be a shift towards [[co-living]] arrangements, especially in expensive cities. So future housing may become smaller and denser, but hopefully smarter, greener and more affordable, adapting to modern needs.

Increasing the supply of housing is fundamental, particularly affordable and social housing built by governments. Reforming planning regulations to allow more construction can help. Measures to [[curb]] speculation, such as taxes on empty properties, may also [[cool prices]]. Rent controls and support for first-time buyers are other options. Essentially, treating housing as a basic need rather than a pure [[investment vehicle]] is key to keeping it accessible and fair.
fixes.why: 'accessible' and 'fair' are plain; marked 'curb', 'cool prices', 'investment vehicle'

fixes.answer: Apartments are generally more affordable, [[low-maintenance]], and often centrally located with good security, which is convenient. The disadvantages are less space and privacy, no garden, and potential noise from neighbours. Houses, by contrast, offer more space, privacy and outdoor areas, ideal for families, but they are more expensive and require more [[upkeep]]. So it is really a [[trade-off]] between convenience and affordability on one hand, and space and privacy on the other.

I partly agree, especially in expensive cities, where it has become genuinely difficult. [[Soaring]] property prices relative to wages, combined with the challenge of saving for a large deposit, have put homeownership [[out of reach]] for many young people, which is a real and worrying shift. However, I would not say it is impossible everywhere. So while it has certainly become far more challenging and requires greater sacrifice, I would not call it entirely [[unattainable]].
fixes.why: 'challenging' and 'sacrifice' are plain; marked 'soaring' and 'out of reach'
